paragraphs.heading: What makes a planet rocky
paragraphs.text: A terrestrial planet is a kind of planet made mostly of silicate, rock or metal. People also call it a rocky, telluric or tellurian planet. The names terrestrial and telluric come from Terra and Tellus, two Latin words for Earth, because these worlds are built much like our own.

paragraphs.heading: The four in our Solar System
paragraphs.text: The International Astronomical Union counts four of them: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, the inner planets nearest the Sun. Astronomers who follow the geophysical definition of a planet also add a few moons that have a planet's mass: Earth's Moon, Io, and sometimes Europa. A few go further and include the big rocky asteroids Pallas and Vesta, though that is rare.

paragraphs.heading: Core, mantle and solid ground
paragraphs.text: Every rocky planet in the Solar System shares one basic layout: a metal core, mostly iron, wrapped in a mantle of silicate rock. Each also has a solid surface. That sets them apart from the bigger gas planets, which are made largely of hydrogen, helium and water in different states. The ground of a rocky planet can carry canyons, craters, mountains and volcanoes. Which of these appear depends on whether a liquid has worn the land down, whether the crust has been moving, or both.

paragraphs.heading: Air that came later
paragraphs.text: The air around a rocky planet is a secondary atmosphere. It was produced either by gas escaping from volcanoes or by debris from comet impacts. The giant planets farther out are different. Their atmospheres are primary, which means they were pulled in directly from the original solar nebula.

paragraphs.heading: Survivors and broken pieces
paragraphs.text: While the Solar System was forming, there were many rocky planetesimals and protoplanets. Most of them either merged into the four rocky planets or were flung away by them. Only Pallas and Vesta came through more or less whole, and both were probably dwarf planets once, before impacts knocked them out of their round shapes. Other bodies began to grow and sort into layers but were wrecked in huge collisions, leaving only a metal core like 16 Psyche or a rocky one like 8 Flora. Many S-type and M-type asteroids may be leftovers of this kind.

paragraphs.heading: Reading a planet's density
paragraphs.text: Uncompressed density is the average density a planet's materials would have with no pressure acting on them. A higher value points to more metal inside. It is not the same as the true average density, because pressure in a planet's core squeezes material and makes it denser. For the round rocky bodies that orbit the Sun directly, uncompressed density gets lower the farther out they are. That pattern matches the temperature gradient thought to have existed in the early solar nebula.

paragraphs.heading: Rocky versus icy
paragraphs.text: Of all these rocky bodies, only Earth has an active hydrosphere at its surface, though Europa is believed to hide one under its ice. From the asteroid belt outward, the round bodies are icy planets instead. Like rocky planets they have solid surfaces, but they are made of ice and rock rather than rock and metal.
